questions.q: Why does self-assessment by a lab evaluating its own model have a structural problem, even assuming good intentions?
options: Because labs are legally barred from evaluating their own models
Because the lab has commercial and reputational incentives tied to a favorable result, which is a conflict of interest independent of anyone's individual good faith
Because internal evaluators are always less technically skilled than external ones
Self-assessment has no real problem as long as the evaluation methodology is sound
questions.explain: The conflict of interest is structural — it exists regardless of how careful or well-intentioned the people running the internal evaluation are, because the incentives still point toward a favorable outcome.

questions.q: What is METR's primary focus, as a third-party evaluator?
options: Persuasion and advertising-related evaluations
Pre-deployment dangerous-capability evaluations focused on long-horizon agentic tasks like autonomous replication, AI R&D acceleration, and cyberattack capability
Running consumer satisfaction surveys for AI products
Certifying that models are completely safe before any release
questions.explain: METR is a nonprofit specializing in long-horizon, agentic dangerous-capability evaluation, run in partnership with frontier labs.

questions.q: What does 'helpful-only model access' grant an external evaluator, and why does it matter?
options: Access to a version of the model with standard safety training not yet applied, letting the evaluator assess underlying capability rather than just guardrailed behavior
A version of the model that only answers helpfully-worded questions
Access limited strictly to the public API, identical to what any user gets
A model that has been fully fine-tuned by the evaluator's own team
questions.explain: Without helpful-only access, an evaluator is only testing the guardrailed surface, which doesn't answer the deeper capability questions dangerous-capability evaluation is meant to address.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is UK AISI's Inspect framework?
options: A proprietary, closed-source testing tool used only internally by UK AISI
An open-source framework for running model evaluations, released so the broader field can build and run evaluations on common, scrutinized infrastructure
A certification stamp that guarantees a model is safe
A dataset of contaminated benchmark questions
questions.explain: Inspect is published openly specifically so evaluation methodology and tooling can be shared and scrutinized across the field, not kept proprietary to one institute.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the current real-world state of third-party evaluation?
options: As a fully mature, standardized certification process that guarantees model safety
As a valuable but still-developing practice, limited by uneven access and a field that itself says the science isn't mature enough to serve as a safety certification
As a practice with no real limitations or access challenges
As something that has been entirely replaced by automated contamination checks
questions.explain: AISI itself has said the science of evaluation isn't mature enough to certify safety, and real access to models for evaluation varies and is often contested, even though external evaluation remains an important structural check.
